hints: Look at the long filamentous virus in the micrograph and measure its length on the page in millimetres with a ruler, from tip to tip.
Remember actual size = image size divided by magnification, then convert your answer from mm to nm using 1 mm = 1 x 10^6 nm.
walkthrough:
**Measure the image size**

Great start, let's get a number to work with. Measure the virus from one end to the other on the printed image.

You should get about $66 \text{ mm}$.

**Use the magnification formula**

Magnification just tells us how many times bigger the image is than the real thing. So we work backwards.

$$\text{actual size} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}} = \frac{66 \text{ mm}}{30\,000} = 0.0022 \text{ mm}$$

**Convert mm to nm and choose**

Viruses are tiny, so we express this in nanometres. Use $1 \text{ mm} = 1 \times 10^6 \text{ nm}$.

$$0.0022 \text{ mm} \times 1 \times 10^6 = 2200 \text{ nm} = 2.2 \times 10^3 \text{ nm}$$

That matches option A perfectly.

options.A: Correct. An image of about 66 mm divided by 30 000 gives 0.0022 mm, which is 2.2 x 10^3 nm.
options.B: Too small by a factor of 10. This would come from a conversion error when changing mm to nm.
options.C: Far too small for this long virus at this magnification. This is 100 times smaller than the true value.
options.D: Far too small, only about 2 nm. This is smaller than a single protein molecule, not a whole virus.
